sections.title: Joint symptoms: building the rheumatological history

blocks.text: In rheumatology the diagnosis is usually reached **at the bedside**: the history and examination make it, and blood tests and imaging mostly confirm it. The history has to pin down **which joints**, **how they behave over the day**, **how the problem started**, and whether there are **features outside the joints**.

blocks.title: Cardinal symptoms to ask about
items: **Joints:** pain, swelling, early-morning stiffness, stiffness after sitting still, reduced movement or function, deformity, weakness, instability, altered sensation
**Eyes and mouth:** dryness of the eyes and mouth, a red eye
**Systemic:** fever, fatigue, weight loss, rash, Raynaud’s phenomenon, diarrhoea, mucosal (e.g. mouth) ulcers

blocks.title: Who is the patient? (demographic clues)
items: **Over 50:** osteoarthritis (OA), polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) and giant cell arteritis. **Under 50:** inflammatory arthritis and autoimmune connective tissue disease are more typical
**Women:** rheumatoid arthritis (RA), Sjögren’s syndrome, SLE and systemic sclerosis. **Men:** gout and ankylosing spondylitis
**Ethnicity:** SLE is commoner in African–Caribbean people
**Occupation:** heavy repetitive use of one region (e.g. lifting) predisposes to soft-tissue pain and OA of the back, hips and knees
**Trauma and stress:** pain causes distress and poor sleep, which raise muscle tension and make the pain worse; bereavement, bullying or job loss can amplify symptoms

blocks.title: Characterising the pain
items: Ask the patient to **point to the pain**. ‘Knee pain’ may come from the popliteal fossa, the joint itself or the bursae around the patella
**Referred pain:** hip disease often presents as pain in the knee or lower thigh, and shoulder pain may spread down the upper arm
**Onset:** sudden (injury, heavy drinking and gout, joint infection or a reactive arthritis after a gut or urinary infection) or gradual and insidious
**Describe the pattern:** articular vs periarticular (tendons, bursae); inflammatory vs non-inflammatory; acute vs chronic; peripheral vs axial (spine, sacroiliac joints)
**Course:** additive (new joints join the old ones), migratory (old joints settle as new ones flare) or palindromic (repeated attacks and relapses)

blocks.note: Look at: the referral map. Pain from the hip spreads to the thigh and knee; shoulder and acromioclavicular pain spreads over the upper arm.

blocks.title: Inflammatory versus mechanical joint pain
rows: Fatigue, fever, rash, Raynaud’s, positive systems review

blocks.text: **Timing the morning stiffness:** more than **30 minutes** points to inflammatory arthritis (Kumar). In RA it usually lasts **an hour or more**, and its length tracks disease activity (Talley). NICE lets you diagnose OA clinically in someone **over 45** with activity-related pain and **no stiffness, or stiffness under 30 minutes**.

blocks.title: Other joint symptoms and what they mean
items: **‘Giving way’:** true dislocation (shoulder, patella), muscle weakness or ligament damage
**Numbness or tingling:** nerve entrapment gives a defined nerve territory; ischaemia does not. Numbness, pins and needles or weakness suggest the nerve is involved
**Sudden new finger deformity:** tendon rupture
**Diabetic cheiroarthritis:** up to half of people with type 1 diabetes. Painful stiff hand joints, especially loss of finger extension, with thick tight skin (probably microangiopathy)

blocks.text: Count the swollen joints first. Davidson calls pain and swelling in **five or more joints or joint groups** a **polyarthritis**. Talley uses monoarthritis (one joint), oligoarthritis (**2–5**) and polyarthritis (**more than 5**). Then ask whether the joints are **hot and swollen** (arthritis) or just painful (arthralgia).

**The textbooks disagree on the polyarthritis cut-off.** Davidson counts **≥ 5** joints or joint groups as polyarthritis, but Talley needs **more than 5** and calls 2–5 joints an oligoarthritis. Use **Davidson’s definition** in the exam.

blocks.title: Acute monoarthritis: telling the causes apart
columns: Clues in the history and examination
rows: **Very fast onset (6–12 h)**, classically the **first MTP joint**. Triggers: alcohol, diuretics, intercurrent illness, dehydration, surgery
Hand/wrist, knee, ankle or hip. Check for primary hyperparathyroidism
Slower onset that **keeps getting worse**. Fever or immunosuppression. Staphylococcal or gonococcal spread, or a penetrating wound
Large effusion straight after injury, no periarticular change. Think of haemophilia in a boy with a family history of bleeding
Recent diarrhoeal illness or genital infection
Gradual pain and stiffness in one joint, **painful but not inflamed**, little swelling

blocks.text: **A single hot joint in a patient with well-controlled RA is septic until proven otherwise**: immunosuppressants hide the usual signs of infection. Aspirating a suspected septic joint is an **emergency**. A **normal serum urate does not rule out gout**.

blocks.title: Acute monoarthritis: what to do
items: **Aspirate the joint (mandatory):** Gram stain, culture, and **polarised light microscopy** for crystals. Take **blood cultures** if sepsis is possible
**Gout:** needle-shaped, **negatively** birefringent urate crystals. **CPPD:** rhomboid, **weakly positively** birefringent crystals
If sepsis is suspected, start **IV antibiotics promptly** while the cultures are pending
Only consider an intra-articular glucocorticoid after **48 hours of negative synovial fluid culture**
Aspiration on its own relieves crystal arthritis

blocks.title: Patterns of polyarthritis
rows: **Symmetrical** small joints of hands and feet (MCP, PIP, wrist, MTP) plus larger joints; upper cervical spine. **DIP spared**
Prolonged morning stiffness, nodules, systemic upset
**Asymmetrical**; PIP **and DIP** joints, large joints, sacroiliac joints
Nail pitting, onycholysis, dactylitis, enthesitis. **The rash may be absent**
Spine, sacroiliac joints, mid-size and large joints, **lower limbs more than upper**
Symmetrical DIP (Heberden’s), PIP (Bouchard’s), **thumb base (first CMC)**, knees, hips, neck and lumbar spine, great-toe MTP
Symmetrical small joints; **arthralgia more than true synovitis**; non-erosive

blocks.text: **The DIP rule:** a hand polyarthritis that **spares the DIP joints** suggests **RA or SLE**. If the **DIPs are involved**, think **OA, gout or psoriatic arthritis**. RA almost never affects the DIPs, so painful swollen DIPs are usually Heberden’s nodes.

blocks.note: Look at: the four joint maps. RA is symmetrical MCP/PIP/MTP; PsA hits PIPs, DIPs and entheses asymmetrically; axial SpA hits the spine, SI joints and large joints; OA hits DIP, PIP, thumb base, knees and hips.

blocks.title: Tests that back up the clinical picture
items: **ANA:** sensitive but not specific (positive in about 95% of SLE, and in some healthy older people). **Anti-dsDNA** is specific for SLE
**Rheumatoid factor:** found in only about **70%** of RA and in some healthy people. **Anti-CCP** has similar sensitivity but is **much more specific**
**HLA-B27:** present in about **90%** of ankylosing spondylitis but also in up to 8% of the healthy population, so it is not a diagnostic test
**2010 ACR/EULAR RA criteria:** a score of **6 or more** means definite RA

sections.title: Back pain, girdle pain and spinal red flags

blocks.text: Most back pain is **mechanical and self-limiting**. The job of the history is to sort it into **mechanical**, **inflammatory** (axial spondyloarthritis) or **destructive** (cancer, infection) pain, and to catch the red flags. **Mechanical pain** causes more than 90% of acute episodes between the ages of 20 and 55, and about **90% of patients recover within 6 weeks**.

blocks.title: Mechanical versus inflammatory back pain
rows: **Wakes the patient at night**, with morning stiffness (at least 30 min)
Lumbosacral region, buttock or upper thigh, **not below the knee**
Sacroiliac and lumbar region; buttock pain that can spread to the back of the thigh
May have uveitis, enthesitis, IBD, psoriasis

blocks.title: Red flags for serious spinal pathology (Davidson)
items: **Age** at onset **under 20 or over 55**
**Constant, progressive pain** that rest does not ease; **thoracic** pain
Past history of **cancer, TB, HIV, systemic glucocorticoids or osteoporosis**
**Systemic upset:** sweats, weight loss; **major trauma**
On examination: painful or severe spinal deformity, **saddle anaesthesia**, progressive neurological signs or wasting, signs at several root levels

blocks.title: Serious causes of back pain and their clues
rows: Pain at rest that **wakes the patient**, present more than 4 weeks, weight loss, known cancer
Fever, immunosuppression, pain worse at rest
Urinary retention or incontinence, faecal incontinence, **saddle anaesthesia**, leg weakness, severe pain
**Sudden** severe pain with little or no trauma, known osteoporosis, steroid use, tenderness over a vertebral body
Leg pain on walking eased by **bending or leaning forward**; foot pulses present (pseudoclaudication)
Pyelonephritis (fever, dysuria), ruptured aortic aneurysm (sudden tearing pain, shock)

blocks.title: Ask about osteoporosis risk factors
items: Menopause
Heavy alcohol use and smoking
Thyroid disease
Chronic kidney or liver disease
Long-term glucocorticoids

blocks.title: Girdle, muscle and neck symptoms
items: **Polymyalgia rheumatica:** pain and stiffness of the **shoulder and hip girdles** after immobility, in patients **over 50** (Talley; Kumar says over 55)
**Inflammatory myositis:** **bilateral proximal weakness** with aching, developing over weeks. Dermatomyositis adds Gottron lesions on the knuckles, a purple eyelid rash and periorbital oedema
**Atlanto-axial subluxation in long-standing RA:** erosion of the transverse ligament behind the dens. Occipital headache and shooting paraesthesia down the arms
**Sciatica:** pain spreading **below the knee** means nerve-root irritation (L4–S1). It is made worse by coughing, straining or leaning forward

blocks.text: **RA neck:** flexing the neck in atlanto-axial subluxation can push the dens into the cord, causing **tetraplegia or sudden death**. This matters most at **intubation for general anaesthesia**, so the RA neck is imaged (MRI) before surgery.

blocks.note: Look at: lateral cervical spine X-ray in RA. The anterior arch of the atlas has slipped forward on the dens of C2 (anterior atlanto-axial subluxation).

sections.title: Extra-articular symptoms, drugs and the rest of the history

blocks.text: Many rheumatic diseases affect **several systems**, so a **full systems review** is part of every rheumatological history. OA and soft-tissue problems rarely cause symptoms outside the joints. A rash, breathlessness, neurological symptoms or a blood disorder suggest a **systemic disease** such as RA, PsA or SLE.

blocks.title: Raynaud’s phenomenon
items: Cold makes the fingers (or toes) go **white, then blue, then red**, from digital vasospasm
**Primary (Raynaud’s disease):** no underlying cause, runs in families, mostly women, **benign**

**Secondary:** systemic sclerosis (may be the first sign; digital ulcers), SLE, mixed connective tissue disease, RA, polymyositis, vasculitis; vibrating tools; **beta-blockers, ergotamine**; vinyl chloride; Buerger’s disease in smokers

blocks.title: Dry eyes and mouth: Sjögren’s syndrome
items: Lymphocytes and plasma cells infiltrate the exocrine glands, which atrophy and scar
Eyes: conjunctivitis, keratitis, corneal ulcers. Mouth: dryness
Beyond the glands: chest infections or interstitial pneumonitis, **renal tubular acidosis**, **nephrogenic diabetes insipidus**, atrophic vaginitis
**Pseudolymphoma** (nodes, splenomegaly) that can rarely progress to **non-Hodgkin lymphoma**
Occurs alone (primary) or with RA and other connective tissue diseases

blocks.text: **Red eye:** **iritis** (painful red eye, injection around the cornea) complicates the **spondyloarthritides and Behçet’s, not RA**. In RA and Sjögren’s a red eye is due to dryness, episcleritis or scleritis.

blocks.title: Other systemic symptoms
items: **Fatigue** is common in connective tissue disease
**Weight loss and diarrhoea** in systemic sclerosis come from small-bowel bacterial overgrowth
**SLE:** fatigue, fever, non-erosive arthritis, photosensitive butterfly rash, mouth ulcers, hair loss, pleuritic pain, Raynaud’s
**Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST):** calcinosis, Raynaud’s, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia
**Fever** can be part of connective tissue disease, especially SLE, but **always exclude infection** first

blocks.title: Drug, past, family and social history
rows: NSAIDs (GI bleeding), DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, leflunomide, hydroxychloroquine), steroids, biologics (serious infection). **Diuretics can precipitate gout**; **steroids can cause avascular necrosis**. A good response to steroids suggests an inflammatory cause
Patients starting biologics are screened for **TB** (chest X-ray, Mantoux test) because TB can reactivate
Recent infection (streptococcal throat, rubella, hepatitis, dysentery, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, parvovirus, TB), **tick bite** (Lyme disease), psoriasis, childhood arthritis, joint trauma or surgery
RA, gout, primary OA, haemochromatosis, spondyloarthritis, IBD, **psoriasis in a first-degree relative** (PsA can come before the rash), **bleeding disorder** (haemarthrosis in a boy)
**Smoking** (RA is commoner in smokers), past STIs, occupation, home set-up, hobbies, and how the disease affects daily life

blocks.title: Functional classes in rheumatoid arthritis
rows: Normal activities possible despite discomfort or limited movement of some joints
Can manage only a few tasks of work or self-care
Complete or near-complete incapacity: bed- or wheelchair-bound

sections.title: Principles of the musculoskeletal examination and the GALS screen

blocks.text: Start examining as the patient **walks in, sits down and undresses**. Watch the gait, any walking aid and how hard dressing is. Then examine each joint in the same order: **look, feel, move** (and **measure**), always **comparing with the other side**.

blocks.title: Look, feel, move
columns: What to do and look for
rows: View the joint from the front, back and sides. Look for erythema, skin atrophy, scars, rash (psoriasis), swelling, deformity, **muscle wasting** (e.g. quadriceps) and symmetry
Warmth with the **back of the fingers**; tenderness along the joint margin while **watching the patient’s face**; then the type of swelling
**Active** range first (full, smooth, painless?), then **passive**. Feel for crepitus and test stability
A goniometer measures from the anatomical zero position; a tape measure records muscle bulk and spinal movement

blocks.title: What the swelling feels like
rows: **Fluctuant**, can be pushed from one part of the joint to another
Fluid: synovial fluid, blood or pus
Osteophytes, e.g. Heberden’s nodes in OA

blocks.title: Active versus passive movement
rows: Pain and restriction in **all directions**, both **active and passive**
Pain only on **active** movement; variable restriction

blocks.title: Terms you must use correctly
items: **Valgus:** the distal part angles **away from the midline** (genu valgum = knock-knees). **Varus:** angled **towards the midline** (genu varum = bow legs)
**Subluxation:** the joint surfaces are displaced but still partly touching. **Dislocation:** they have lost contact completely
**Fixed flexion deformity:** the joint cannot be fully straightened. A knee recorded as ‘30° to 60°’ has a 30° fixed flexion deformity and bends only to 60°
**Crepitus:** grating from irregular joint surfaces, a sign of chronic damage
Deformity and muscle wasting both mean **chronic** disease

blocks.title: Grading tenderness
rows: Says it hurts, winces and pulls the joint away
Will not let you touch it

blocks.title: Typical findings in an osteoarthritic joint
items: Marginal osteophytes (bony swellings, e.g. Heberden’s nodes)
Little or no synovitis
Deformity but little instability
Reduced active and passive movement
Crepitus and joint-line tenderness
Wasting and weakness of nearby muscles

blocks.title: The GALS screen (gait, arms, legs, spine)
columns: What the patient does / what you do
rows: Any pain or stiffness in the joints, muscles or back? Any trouble **dressing and washing**, **using stairs** or **getting out of a chair**?
Walk away, turn, come back: stride, smoothness, turning, limp or pain

Hands behind the head (shoulders); arms straight out, palms down then up; **make a fist**, then **touch each fingertip with the thumb**; **squeeze across the MCPs** (synovitis); press over supraspinatus (hyperalgesia)
Flex each hip and knee and **rotate the hip internally** (early OA), feel for knee crepitus, warmth and effusion; **squeeze across the MTPs**; inspect the feet

Inspect from behind and the side (scoliosis, kyphosis, lordosis); touch toes (Schober’s); slide hand down the side of the leg; ear to shoulder; chin to chest and look at the ceiling; turn the trunk with the pelvis fixed

blocks.text: GALS is a **screen**. Any joint that looks or moves abnormally then needs a full **regional look–feel–move examination**.

blocks.note: Look at: each GALS step, including the MCP and MTP squeeze, pressing on supraspinatus, internal rotation of the hip, and Davidson’s 10 cm to 15 cm Schöber marks.

cite.figure: Clinical exam of the MSK system

blocks.note: Look at: the inspection checklist (extensor surfaces, face, hands, trunk, legs, feet) with examples of Heberden’s nodes, RA synovitis, malar rash, scleritis and acute gout.

blocks.text: Sit the patient with **both hands palm-down on a pillow**. Do a **general inspection** first (Cushingoid face, eye inflammation, other joints). Then look at the **dorsum** (wrists, MCPs, PIPs and DIPs, nails), **feel and move** each joint, turn the hands over to look at the **palms**, test **function** (grip, key grip, opposition), and finish at the **elbows**.

blocks.title: Deformities of the rheumatoid hand
rows: Fingers drift towards the ulnar side at the MCP joints, usually with **volar (palmar) subluxation**
**PIP fixed in flexion**, **DIP hyperextended**: the PIP pokes through a torn central extensor slip
Thumb IP joint hyperextended, MCP joint flexed and subluxed

blocks.note: Look at: rheumatoid hands with ulnar deviation, a Z thumb, swan neck fingers and boutonnière deformity.

blocks.title: Hand signs that point to a diagnosis
rows: Heberden’s (DIP) and Bouchard’s (PIP) nodes; squared thumb base (first CMC)
Nail pitting, onycholysis, ridging; **dactylitis** (sausage digit); DIP disease
Tight shiny skin, lost pulp fat pads, **digital ulcers**, calcinosis, telangiectasia

blocks.note: Look at: OA hand with Heberden’s nodes over the DIP joints and Bouchard’s nodes over the PIP joints.
Look at: psoriatic nails showing pitting, ridging, onycholysis and discoloration.

blocks.title: Feel and move: wrist and fingers
items: Normal wrist range: about **75°** dorsiflexion and **75°** palmar flexion, about **20°** radial and ulnar deviation
**Ulnar styloid** tenderness: RA. Tenderness at the **tip of the radial styloid**: **de Quervain’s tenosynovitis**, worse when the thumb is folded into the palm
**Anatomical snuffbox** tenderness: first CMC arthritis or **scaphoid injury**
MCP joints are felt best at **90° flexion**. Rocking the proximal phalanx shows volar subluxation or laxity
**Palmar tendon crepitus** as the fingers flex and extend means **flexor tenosynovitis**
**Trigger finger:** a tender nodule in the **distal palm**; the finger catches in flexion and releases with a snap. RA and diabetes are causes

blocks.title: Carpal tunnel syndrome
rows: Wakes at night with numbness, tingling and pain in the **median nerve territory** (radial three and a half fingers)
**Thenar wasting**, sensory loss in the median territory
Hold both wrists flexed for **30 seconds**: paraesthesia appears. **More reliable than Tinel’s**
Tapping over the flexor retinaculum reproduces the tingling
RA, hypothyroidism, acromegaly, pregnancy, diabetes, amyloidosis, gout, obesity, wrist-flexed work; often idiopathic

blocks.text: Even when asked to examine **only the hands**, look at the **extensor surface of the elbows** for **rheumatoid nodules, gouty tophi and psoriatic plaques**.
Don’t mix up the finger deformities. **Swan neck:** the PIP bends **backwards** and the DIP is flexed. **Boutonnière:** the PIP is **flexed** and the DIP bends backwards. Name the PIP position first.

blocks.note: Look at: rheumatoid vasculitis. Small dark infarcts at the nail folds show active disease.

sections.title: Examining the spine, hips, knees and shoulders

blocks.title: Thoracolumbar spine
items: Stand the patient in underwear. Inspect from **behind and the side**. **Loss of lumbar lordosis and thoracic kyphosis** is typical of ankylosing spondylitis. Look for scoliosis
A scoliosis caused by **unequal leg length** reduces on **sitting or lying**
Feel each spinous process for tenderness and the paraspinal muscles for spasm

**Bending** happens mainly at the lumbar spine and **rotation** at the thoracic spine. **Lateral flexion** is lost **early** in AS. In advanced AS the spine is flat and rigid, so all bending happens at the hips

blocks.title: Schober’s test: two versions
rows: Midline mark about 4 cm below the level of the iliac crests, second mark **10 cm above** it
On bending forward the gap opens to **15 cm** (about 5 cm increase)
Mark at L5 (level of the posterior iliac spines); points **5 cm below and 10 cm above** (15 cm apart)
Gap should reach **20 cm or more**; an increase **under 5 cm** means restricted lumbar flexion

blocks.text: **Schober’s numbers differ between books.** Davidson starts with marks **10 cm** apart that should stretch to **15 cm**. Talley and Zero to Finals start at **15 cm** apart and expect **20 cm**. Both look for an increase of about **5 cm**. Follow **Davidson** in the exam and don’t mix the two.

blocks.note: Look at: Talley’s Schober marks, 5 cm below and 10 cm above L5, separating to 20 cm or more on full flexion.

blocks.title: Nerve root and sacroiliac tests
rows: Patient supine; lift the straight leg (normal 80–90°)
Ipsilateral leg pain past the knee, worse with **ankle dorsiflexion**: lower lumbar (L4–S1) root compression. Limited below 60° has about 91% sensitivity
Pain in the affected leg: **large or central** disc prolapse
Press the two ASISs apart, or FABER (figure-4) and push on the knee
Pain over the sacroiliac joint: sacroiliitis

blocks.title: Lumbar root signs
rows: Outer calf, top and inner side of the foot
Back of the calf, **lateral border of the foot**

blocks.title: Hip examination
rows: Gait, scars, a rotated leg. Joint tenderness just below the **midpoint of the inguinal ligament**; compare the levels of the greater trochanters
Internal and external rotation about **45°**, abduction **50°**, adduction **45°**, extension about **30°**
**Internal rotation**, abduction and extension are usually restricted. Pain and limitation on internally rotating the flexed hip appear early
Fully flex both hips to flatten the lumbar lordosis, then straighten one leg. If it **won’t lie flat**, there is a **hidden fixed flexion deformity**
Stand on one leg. Normally the opposite (lifted) side of the pelvis rises. With **disease of the standing hip** or proximal myopathy, the **lifted side sags**
**True:** ASIS to medial malleolus (shorter side = hip disease). **Apparent:** umbilicus to medial malleolus (pelvic tilt)
A fall, cannot bear weight, leg **shortened and externally rotated**

blocks.title: Knee examination
rows: Examine the **normal knee first**. Look for quadriceps wasting, scars and swelling. **Varus** deformity usually means **OA**, **valgus** usually means **RA**
Empty the suprapatellar pouch with one hand, then push the patella down: it sinks and taps the femur. Detects **large** effusions
Stroke fluid out of one side of the knee, then the other, and watch for a bulge on the first side. Detects **small** effusions
More than **5–10°** of collateral or cruciate laxity is abnormal. **Lachman’s test** (knee flexed 20–30°) is the best bedside test for an ACL tear (LR+ 42); anterior drawer LR+ 37
**Baker’s cyst**: if it ruptures it **mimics DVT**, sometimes with bruising below the malleoli (crescent sign). A popliteal aneurysm is **pulsatile**

blocks.note: Look at: (a) the patellar tap and (b) the bulge sign, with the suprapatellar pouch being compressed.

blocks.title: Shoulder pain on examination
rows: **Painful arc**: pain peaks in mid-abduction and eases as the arm reaches full elevation. Passive elevation hurts less. Some rotation is kept
Cannot **start** active abduction, but can hold the arm up once it is lifted
Severe pain and shrinking range at first, then a ‘frozen’ phase with **all movements lost**, including rotation, but little pain
Pins and needles or neurological signs in the arm

blocks.note: Look at: a Baker’s cyst seen from behind as a swelling in the popliteal fossa of the right knee.

cards.front: How long does morning stiffness last in inflammatory arthritis?
cards.back: More than 30 minutes (Kumar). In RA it usually lasts an hour or more, and the longer it lasts, the more active the disease (Talley).

cards.front: Pain worse with use and eased by rest, or worse after rest and eased by use: which is mechanical?
cards.back: Worse with use and eased by rest is mechanical (e.g. OA). Worse after rest and better with activity is inflammatory.

cards.front: A patient has knee pain but the knee examines normally. What should you examine next?
cards.back: The hip. Hip disease often refers pain to the knee and lower thigh.

cards.front: Davidson’s definition of polyarthritis?
cards.back: Pain and swelling in 5 or more joints or joint groups. Talley uses more than 5, and calls 2–5 joints an oligoarthritis.

cards.front: What does a monoarthritis that reaches its peak within 6–12 hours suggest?
cards.back: Crystal arthritis (gout, pseudogout). Septic arthritis comes on more slowly and keeps getting worse until treated.

cards.front: A patient with well-controlled RA on immunosuppressants develops one hot joint. What do you assume, and what do you do?
cards.back: Assume septic arthritis, because immunosuppressants mask infection. Aspirate the joint urgently.

cards.front: What does a hand polyarthritis that spares the DIP joints suggest?
cards.back: RA or SLE. If the DIPs are involved, think of OA, gout or psoriatic arthritis.

cards.front: What age at onset of back pain is a red flag (Davidson)?
cards.back: Under 20 or over 55 years.

cards.front: Name the symptoms of cauda equina syndrome.
cards.back: Urinary retention or incontinence, faecal incontinence, saddle anaesthesia and leg weakness.

cards.front: Shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness in a patient over 50. What is the diagnosis?
cards.back: Polymyalgia rheumatica (Kumar uses over 55).

cards.front: Which arthritides cause iritis (anterior uveitis), and which classic one does not?
cards.back: Spondyloarthritides and Behçet’s cause iritis. RA does not: its red eye is episcleritis, scleritis or dryness.

cards.front: What is the colour sequence in Raynaud’s phenomenon?
cards.back: White, then blue, then red on cold exposure.

cards.front: What must be screened for before starting a biologic?
cards.back: Tuberculosis (chest X-ray, Mantoux test), because biologics can reactivate TB.

cards.front: Pain on both active and passive movement, or pain on active movement only: what does each suggest?
cards.back: Both suggests an articular (joint) problem. Active only suggests a periarticular lesion such as a tendon or bursa.

cards.front: How do synovitis, an effusion and a bony swelling feel?
cards.back: Synovitis is soft and boggy. An effusion is fluctuant and can be shifted. Bony swelling is hard and fixed (osteophytes).

cards.front: What does a knee recorded as ‘25° to 90°’ mean?
cards.back: A 25° fixed flexion deformity, with flexion possible to 90°.

cards.front: Swan neck vs boutonnière deformity?
cards.back: Swan neck: PIP hyperextended, DIP flexed. Boutonnière: PIP flexed, DIP hyperextended.

cards.front: How is Phalen’s test done, and how does it compare with Tinel’s sign?
cards.back: Hold both wrists flexed for 30 seconds; median-territory paraesthesia is positive. It is more reliable than Tinel’s sign.

cards.front: What does Thomas’s test detect?
cards.back: A fixed flexion deformity of the hip that an increased lumbar lordosis is hiding.

cards.front: Patellar tap vs bulge sign?
cards.back: The patellar tap shows large effusions; the bulge sign shows small ones.

cards.front: What is a normal Schober’s result in Davidson’s version?
cards.back: Marks 10 cm apart separate to 15 cm on bending forward.

cards.front: What does a positive Trendelenburg test look like, and what does it mean?
cards.back: Standing on the affected leg, the opposite (lifted) side of the pelvis sags. It means disease of the standing hip or proximal myopathy.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has had painful, swollen hands for three months. Each morning her fingers are stiff for about an hour and a half, and they loosen up as she uses them during the day.
items.explanation: Prolonged morning stiffness (well over 30 minutes) that eases with use, plus swelling, is the inflammatory pattern. Its length reflects disease activity.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man has pain in the front of the right lower thigh and knee when he walks. The right knee has no effusion and a full, painless range, but internally rotating the flexed right hip reproduces his pain.
items.explanation: Two steps: the knee is normal, so look elsewhere. Pain on hip internal rotation (lost early in OA) shows the problem is in the hip, which commonly refers pain to the knee and lower thigh.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has had type 1 diabetes since childhood. Her fingers have become painful and she can no longer straighten them fully. The skin over her hands is thick and tight, and no joint is swollen.
items.explanation: Up to half of people with type 1 diabetes develop cheiroarthritis: painful, restricted hand joints with loss of finger extension and thickened tight skin, probably from microangiopathy.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has seropositive rheumatoid arthritis that has been well controlled on methotrexate and a TNF inhibitor. For two days his right knee has been hot, red and swollen, and he cannot bear weight. His temperature is 37.4 °C and no other joints are active.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Aspirate the knee for Gram stain, culture and crystal microscopy
Increase the methotrexate dose for an RA flare
Arrange a knee X-ray and review in one week
questions.explanation: One hot joint in a patient with well-controlled RA must be treated as **septic** until proven otherwise. Immunosuppressants (methotrexate, biologics) blunt fever and other signs of sepsis, so a near-normal temperature is no reassurance. Aspirating a suspected septic joint is an **emergency**: send fluid for Gram stain, culture and polarised microscopy, and take blood cultures.
whyNot: A single hot joint while the rest of the RA is quiet is not a typical flare. Treating it as one and increasing immunosuppression could make an infection worse.
Steroid injection is only considered after 48 hours of negative synovial fluid culture, because injecting an infected joint is dangerous.
A normal or raised urate neither confirms nor excludes gout, and it does not address the possibility of sepsis.
Imaging cannot identify an organism, and waiting a week delays treatment of a possible septic joint. Suspected sepsis needs aspiration now.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man has painful swelling of his left knee, his right ankle and the distal interphalangeal joints of two fingers on his right hand. His left second toe is swollen along its whole length. Several of his fingernails have small pits. He has never noticed a rash.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The pattern is **asymmetrical**, involves **DIP joints** and a **sausage digit (dactylitis)**, and there is **nail pitting**. All of these point to psoriatic arthritis. The skin disease may be **absent** when the arthritis starts, so ask about psoriasis in first-degree relatives.
whyNot: RA is symmetrical, affects MCPs and PIPs and spares the DIPs. Dactylitis and nail pitting are not features.
Nodal OA causes hard bony DIP/PIP swellings, not a swollen whole toe or an inflamed knee and ankle in a 41-year-old.
Chronic gout affects distal joints after a history of acute attacks. Nail pitting and dactylitis point elsewhere.
SLE causes a symmetrical small-joint arthralgia, usually with little synovitis and no DIP or nail changes.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Lumbar disc prolapse with root compression

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has had low back and buttock pain for six months. It wakes him in the early hours, he is stiff for about an hour each morning, and he feels much better after training at the gym. He also has pain under his heels.
items.explanation: Gradual onset before 40, night pain, long morning stiffness and **improvement with exercise** are inflammatory back pain. The heel pain is enthesitis (plantar fasciitis), which also points to axial SpA.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman who has taken prednisolone for COPD for years feels sudden severe mid-back pain as she lifts a bag of shopping. She is tender over a single thoracic vertebra and has no neurological deficit.
items.explanation: Sudden pain after little or no trauma, plus steroid use (an osteoporosis risk), suggests a crush fracture. Point tenderness over a vertebral body supports it.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man gets aching in both buttocks and legs after walking about 200 m. It eases when he sits down or leans forward on a shopping trolley. Both foot pulses are easily felt.
items.explanation: Two steps: walking-related leg pain could be vascular claudication, but **palpable pulses** and relief by **bending forward** point to pseudoclaudication from spinal stenosis.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has had gritty, dry eyes for two years and needs water to swallow dry food. Blood tests show a metabolic acidosis due to renal tubular acidosis.
questions.leadIn: Which complication is she at greatest risk of in the long term?
questions.explanation: Dry eyes and mouth with **renal tubular acidosis** point to **Sjögren’s syndrome**: lymphocytes and plasma cells infiltrate the exocrine glands. Its **pseudolymphoma** (lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly) can progress, rarely, to a true **non-Hodgkin lymphoma**.
whyNot: Aortic root disease is linked to HLA-B27 spondyloarthritis.
Anterior uveitis complicates spondyloarthritis and Behçet’s. In Sjögren’s the eye problem is dryness (keratitis, conjunctivitis).
Atlanto-axial subluxation is a complication of long-standing RA.
Bacterial overgrowth with weight loss and diarrhoea is a feature of systemic sclerosis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with two years of inflammatory low back pain develops a painful red left eye. The redness is concentrated around the cornea and spreads out from the pupil.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely eye complication?
questions.explanation: Iritis (anterior uveitis) gives a painful red eye, worst **around the cornea**. It complicates the **spondyloarthritides** (and Behçet’s), but **not RA**.
whyNot: Scleritis is linked to RA and vasculitis, not axial SpA.
Episcleritis is a typical complication of RA, not of spondyloarthritis.
Dry eyes are the Sjögren’s pattern.
Conjunctivitis goes with reactive arthritis. The painful circumcorneal redness here points to iritis.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A woman with active rheumatoid arthritis has soft, spongy swelling around several MCP joints. The swelling is not fluctuant and cannot be pushed from one side of the joint to the other.
items.explanation: Boggy, rubbery swelling that does not fluctuate is thickened inflamed synovium. An effusion would be fluctuant and could be shifted; bony swelling would be hard.

items.stem: A painter has shoulder pain only when he lifts his arm himself. When the examiner moves the arm through its whole range while he relaxes, there is no pain or restriction.
items.explanation: Pain only on **active** movement with full painless **passive** movement suggests a periarticular structure (e.g. rotator cuff tendon or bursa) rather than the joint itself.

items.stem: A goniometer reading of a man’s right knee is recorded as ‘20° to 100°’.
items.explanation: Range is measured from the anatomical zero. Starting at 20° means the knee cannot straighten beyond 20°, which is a **20° fixed flexion deformity**. It then flexes to 100°.

items.stem: When a 74-year-old woman with long-standing knee osteoarthritis stands, her knees bow outwards so that there is a wide gap between them while her ankles touch.
items.explanation: Bow legs are genu varum: the distal segment angles towards the midline. Varus knees usually mean OA; valgus (knock-knees) is more typical of RA.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman has had rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years. One of her fingers is held with the proximal interphalangeal joint bent in fixed flexion and the distal interphalangeal joint hyperextended.
questions.leadIn: What is this deformity called?
questions.explanation: A **boutonnière (buttonhole) deformity** is a **flexed PIP with a hyperextended DIP**. It happens when the PIP joint pushes through a torn central slip of the extensor tendon.
whyNot: Swan neck is the reverse: PIP hyperextended and DIP flexed.
The Z thumb affects the thumb (IP hyperextension, MCP flexion), not a finger.
Ulnar deviation is drift of the fingers at the MCP joints, not a PIP/DIP posture.
Trigger finger is a tendon that catches in flexion and releases with a snap. It is not a fixed PIP/DIP deformity.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with hypothyroidism wakes most nights with tingling and pain in her thumb, index and middle fingers. She shakes her hand to relieve it.
questions.leadIn: Which bedside test is the most reliable way to reproduce her symptoms?
options: Holding both wrists fully flexed for 30 seconds
Pressing on the tip of the radial styloid
Feeling the palm while she flexes and extends her fingers
questions.explanation: This is **carpal tunnel syndrome** (night-time symptoms in the median territory; hypothyroidism is a cause). **Phalen’s test**, holding the wrists flexed for 30 seconds, reproduces the paraesthesia and is **more reliable than Tinel’s sign**.
whyNot: That is Tinel’s sign. It can be positive, but Talley rates it less reliable than Phalen’s test.
Tenderness at the radial styloid tip is the sign of de Quervain’s tenosynovitis.
Snuffbox tenderness suggests first CMC arthritis or a scaphoid injury.
Palmar tendon crepitus detects flexor tenosynovitis or trigger finger, not median nerve compression.

questions.theme: Special tests in the spine and lower limb
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Lateral compression of the iliac spines

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with hip osteoarthritis lies flat on the couch with both legs straight. His lumbar spine is noticeably arched. You want to show whether the hip has a fixed flexion deformity.
items.explanation: Increased lumbar lordosis can hide a hip fixed flexion deformity. Thomas’s test flexes both hips to flatten the pelvis, then extends one leg. If it will not lie flat, there is a fixed flexion deformity.

items.stem: A 25-year-old footballer twisted his knee and it swelled within an hour. You want the most accurate bedside test for an anterior cruciate ligament tear, done with the knee bent 20–30°.
items.explanation: Lachman’s test is done at 20–30° of flexion with a forward tug on the tibia. It has the higher likelihood ratio (LR+ 42) compared with the anterior drawer test (LR+ 37).

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman’s knee looks slightly full beside the patella. The patellar tap is negative, but you still suspect a small amount of fluid.
items.explanation: The patellar tap detects only large effusions. The bulge sign (stroke fluid out of one side, then watch it bulge back after stroking the other) detects small ones.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 23-year-old man had bloody diarrhoea two weeks ago. Now his left knee and right ankle are painful and swollen, and both eyes are red and sticky.
items.explanation: Arthritis that follows a gut (or genital) infection is reactive arthritis. Conjunctivitis is its typical eye feature. It favours large lower-limb joints.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman develops a hot, swollen wrist two days after a hip replacement. Fluid aspirated from the wrist contains rhomboid crystals that are weakly positively birefringent. Gram stain is negative.
items.explanation: Rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals are calcium pyrophosphate. Surgery and intercurrent illness are classic triggers of crystal arthritis. Gout crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has painful small joints in both hands but no obvious swelling. She also has a facial rash that gets worse in the sun, mouth ulcers and patchy hair loss.
items.explanation: SLE causes symmetrical small-joint arthralgia with little true synovitis. Photosensitive rash, oral ulcers and alopecia are typical multisystem features.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman has had aching and stiffness in both shoulders and hips for three weeks. It is worst in the mornings, and she struggles to get out of bed or comb her hair. Her small joints are normal.
items.explanation: Shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness after immobility, in someone over 50, is polymyalgia rheumatica. Small joints are spared.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has had rheumatoid arthritis for 20 years and is booked for elective surgery under general anaesthetic. She mentions occipital headaches and shooting pins and needles down both arms when she bends her neck forward.
questions.leadIn: What is the most important step before her anaesthetic?
options: Nerve conduction studies of the median nerve
questions.explanation: Long-standing RA can erode the **transverse ligament** behind the dens, causing **atlanto-axial subluxation**. Occipital headache and arm paraesthesia on neck flexion are warning symptoms. Neck flexion during **intubation** could compress the cord (tetraplegia, sudden death), so the cervical spine is imaged first (lateral X-ray, MRI).
whyNot: Hand X-rays show erosions but do not affect anaesthetic safety.
Anti-CCP helps diagnose RA, which is already established. It says nothing about the neck.
Symptoms in both arms on neck flexion point to the cervical cord, not carpal tunnel syndrome.
Schober’s test measures lumbar flexion, not cervical instability.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old warehouse worker developed low back pain while lifting a heavy box three days ago. The pain is in his lower back and upper buttock.
questions.leadIn: Which additional feature most urgently needs further investigation?
options: Pain that eases when he lies still
Pain limited to the back and upper thigh
Spasm of the paraspinal muscles on one side
Two similar episodes in the past that settled
Numbness around the anus and new difficulty passing urine
questions.explanation: **Saddle anaesthesia** with **urinary retention** suggests **cauda equina syndrome** (usually a large central disc), which needs **urgent investigation** and neurosurgical referral. The other features are typical of mechanical back pain.
whyNot: Relief with rest is a mechanical feature. Destructive pain does not settle with rest.
Pain confined to the back and upper leg, not below the knee, fits mechanical pain.
One-sided paraspinal spasm is a common examination finding in mechanical back pain.
Recurrent episodes are typical of mechanical pain.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has had low back pain for six months.
questions.leadIn: Which feature most strongly suggests an inflammatory rather than a mechanical cause?
options: Pain worse with activity and better with rest
Morning stiffness that eases with exercise
Pain limited to the lumbar region
questions.explanation: Inflammatory back pain from axial SpA starts gradually **before age 40**, wakes the patient at night, causes **morning stiffness** and **gets better with exercise**. Mechanical pain does the opposite: it is eased by rest and often starts suddenly after lifting.
whyNot: Worse with activity and better with rest is the mechanical pattern.
Sudden onset when lifting is typical of mechanical pain.
About 90% of mechanical episodes resolve within six weeks. Inflammatory pain persists.
Site alone does not separate them. Both can be lumbar.

questions.stem: During a GALS screen of a 48-year-old woman with early-morning stiffness in her feet, you want to test for metatarsophalangeal synovitis.
questions.leadIn: Which manoeuvre is most appropriate?
options: Asking her to touch her toes
Asking her to make a tight fist
questions.explanation: In GALS, a **squeeze across the forefoot** (and across the MCPs in the hands) causes pain when the MTP (or MCP) joints are inflamed. It is a quick screen for early inflammatory arthritis.
whyNot: Hip internal rotation screens for hip disease (pain and restriction occur early in OA).
Toe touching assesses lumbar and hip flexion.
Making a fist tests hand function and finger flexion.
Pressing on supraspinatus checks for widespread hyperalgesia, not synovitis.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man has inflammatory back pain. Using Davidson’s method, you make a midline mark a few centimetres below the line of the iliac crests and a second mark 10 cm above it. When he bends forward as far as he can, the marks are 12 cm apart.
questions.leadIn: How should this be interpreted?
options: Restricted lumbar flexion, supporting axial spondyloarthritis
Restricted hip flexion from a hidden fixed flexion deformity
questions.explanation: **Step 1, know the normal:** in Davidson’s version, marks 10 cm apart should separate to **15 cm** on full forward flexion, an increase of about 5 cm. **Step 2, compare:** 12 cm is an increase of only 2 cm, so lumbar flexion is restricted. **Step 3, apply it:** in a young man with inflammatory back pain, this supports **axial SpA/AS**. **Watch the other version:** Talley and Zero to Finals start 15 cm apart and expect 20 cm or more. The abnormal finding is the same: an increase of less than about 5 cm.
whyNot: A 2 cm increase is well below the expected 5 cm (10 cm to 15 cm).
A hidden hip fixed flexion deformity is found with Thomas’s test. Schober’s measures the lumbar spine only.
Root compression is tested with the straight leg raise, not by skin marks on the back.
Thoracic rotation is tested with the patient seated and turning the trunk. Schober’s measures lumbar flexion.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man takes bendroflumethiazide for hypertension. Over eight hours his right big-toe joint has become red, shiny, swollen and too painful to touch. His temperature is 37.6 °C. His serum urate is within the normal range.
questions.leadIn: What is the best next step to establish the diagnosis?
options: Conclude that gout is excluded by the normal urate
Aspirate the joint and examine the fluid under polarised light, with Gram stain and culture
Inject a glucocorticoid into the joint straight away
Request a plain X-ray to look for crystals
questions.explanation: **Step 1, the pattern:** very rapid onset (6–12 hours) in the **first MTP joint**, in a man on a **diuretic**, is classic gout. **Step 2, the trap:** a **normal serum urate does not exclude gout**. **Step 3, confirm and exclude sepsis:** joint aspiration is **mandatory** in acute monoarthritis. Polarised microscopy shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals, and Gram stain and culture rule out septic arthritis, the key differential.
whyNot: Urate can be normal during an acute attack, so a normal level cannot rule gout out.
Anti-CCP supports RA, which rarely presents as an acute first-MTP monoarthritis.
Steroid injection is only considered after 48 hours of negative culture, because sepsis has not been excluded.
A plain X-ray cannot show urate crystals. Aspiration and microscopy identify them.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman walks with a lurch. When she stands on her right leg, the left side of her pelvis drops. When she stands on her left leg, the right side of her pelvis rises normally.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely interpretation?
options: Right hip joint disease, or weakness of the muscles that stabilise it
Fixed flexion deformity of the left hip
Apparent leg-length difference from pelvic tilt
questions.explanation: **Step 1, the normal response:** when you stand on one leg, the pelvis on the **lifted (non-weight-bearing) side rises**. **Step 2, the abnormal:** if the standing hip is diseased, or its muscles are weak (e.g. proximal myopathy), the lifted side **sags**. **Step 3, locate it:** she sags on the left while **standing on the right**, so the problem is the **right hip**. The test is normal when she stands on the left.
whyNot: When she stands on the left leg the pelvis behaves normally, so the left hip is supporting her well.
A fixed flexion deformity is found with Thomas’s test and does not make the pelvis drop in this way.
Apparent leg-length differences come from pelvic tilt and are measured from the umbilicus. They do not explain a one-sided Trendelenburg sign.
A knee effusion would not make the pelvis sag on single-leg stance.

questions.theme: Signs in the hands and wrists
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Sclerodactyly with loss of pulp fat pads

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman has Raynaud’s phenomenon and difficulty swallowing. The skin of her fingers is tight and shiny with no normal creases, the finger pads look shrunken, and there are small ulcers at two fingertips.
items.explanation: Tight, shiny skin with loss of pulp fat and digital ulcers is sclerodactyly. With Raynaud’s and oesophageal dysmotility, it points to systemic sclerosis.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with active rheumatoid arthritis has several tiny black-brown spots, about 1–2 mm across, at the edges of his nail folds.
items.explanation: Small dark nail-fold infarcts mean active vasculitis, typically in RA. Splinter haemorrhages lie under the nail in the nail bed.

items.stem: A woman who recently had a baby has pain on the thumb side of her wrist when she lifts the baby. She is tender at the tip of the radial styloid, and folding her thumb into her palm makes the pain worse.
items.explanation: Pain and tenderness at the radial styloid, worse when the thumb is flexed into the palm, is de Quervain’s tenosynovitis (abductor pollicis longus tendon sheath).

items.stem: A 56-year-old man with diabetes finds his ring finger stays bent when he wakes. He has to pull it straight, when it releases with a click. A tender lump can be felt in his distal palm.
items.explanation: A thickened flexor tendon nodule in the distal palm catches, then releases with a snap. This is trigger finger, which is commoner in diabetes and RA.

questions.theme: Clues from the past, family and drug history
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy has a tense, swollen knee after a minor fall in the playground. His mother says her brother had ‘bleeds into his joints’ as a child.
items.explanation: Two steps: a large effusion soon after a minor injury suggests haemarthrosis, and an affected maternal uncle suggests an X-linked bleeding disorder. A family history of bleeding disorder explains an acutely swollen joint in a boy.

items.stem: A 39-year-old man has an asymmetrical arthritis of several DIP joints and one swollen whole finger. He has no skin rash, but his father has psoriasis.
items.explanation: The arthritis of psoriatic arthritis can come before the rash. A first-degree relative with psoriasis, DIP disease and dactylitis are the clues.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with SLE has taken high-dose prednisolone for a long time. She develops sudden, severe groin pain and cannot bear weight on that leg. There was no fall.
items.explanation: Long-term steroids are a classic cause of avascular necrosis. Sudden hip pain with inability to bear weight, and no fall to suggest a fracture, fits aseptic necrosis of the femoral head.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has painful, swollen joints. On examination her left knee, right ankle and left wrist are swollen. No other joints are affected.
questions.leadIn: Using Talley’s classification by number of joints, how is this best described?
questions.explanation: Talley counts **one** joint as monoarthritis, **2–5** as **oligoarthritis**, and **more than 5** as polyarthritis. Three swollen joints is an oligoarthritis. (Davidson calls 5 or more joints a polyarthritis.)
whyNot: Monoarthritis is a single joint.
Polyarthritis needs more than 5 joints in Talley’s scheme, or 5 or more in Davidson’s.
Arthralgia means joint pain without swelling or redness. These joints are swollen.
Enthesitis is inflammation where a tendon or ligament attaches to bone, not swelling of a joint.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman who has had rheumatoid arthritis for many years is examined standing. Her knees angle inwards so that they touch, while her ankles are far apart.
questions.leadIn: Which deformity does she have?
questions.explanation: **Knock-knees** are **genu valgum**: the distal part (the leg) angles **away from the midline**. Valgus knees are more typical of **RA**, and varus (bow legs) of **OA**.
whyNot: Genu varum is bow legs, with the knees apart. It is typical of OA.
A fixed flexion deformity is failure to straighten the knee, best seen from the side.
Patellar subluxation is the patella slipping laterally as the knee flexes. It does not change knee alignment.
A Baker’s cyst is a swelling in the popliteal fossa, not an angular deformity.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with knee osteoarthritis develops sudden pain and swelling in his right calf. Two days later a crescent of bruising appears below his medial malleolus.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause?
options: Fixed flexion deformity of the knee
questions.explanation: A Baker’s (popliteal) cyst is a pressure diverticulum of the synovium behind the knee. When it **ruptures** into the calf it **mimics a DVT**, and bruising below the malleoli (the **crescent sign**) is a useful clue.
whyNot: A popliteal aneurysm is a pulsatile mass in the popliteal fossa. It does not cause bruising below the ankle.
A torn meniscus causes knee locking and swelling, not calf pain and ankle bruising.
Septic arthritis gives a hot, swollen, very tender knee with fever, not calf swelling and bruising.
A fixed flexion deformity is a loss of extension, not an acute calf swelling.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man on furosemide wakes after a night of heavy drinking with an excruciating, red, swollen big-toe joint that has peaked within hours. Fluid aspirated from the joint contains needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals.
items.explanation: Very fast onset in the first MTP joint, with alcohol and a diuretic as triggers. Needle-shaped negatively birefringent urate crystals confirm gout.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man who takes long-term prednisolone has a knee that has become steadily more painful and swollen over three days. His temperature is 39 °C. Aspirated fluid is opaque and Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci.
items.explanation: Gradual but relentless worsening with fever, in an immunosuppressed patient, and organisms on Gram stain mean septic arthritis. Staphylococci are the classic Gram-positive cause.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man’s knee swells tensely within an hour of a hard tackle in a football match. There is no redness of the overlying skin. Aspiration yields uniformly bloodstained fluid.
items.explanation: Rapid swelling straight after injury, a large effusion without periarticular change, and blood on aspiration mean haemarthrosis (from a fracture or a ligament tear).

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with active rheumatoid arthritis despite methotrexate is about to start a TNF-inhibitor biologic. You review her treatment history.
questions.leadIn: Which test is most important before the biologic is started?
questions.explanation: Biologics can **reactivate latent tuberculosis**, so patients are screened first with a **chest X-ray and Mantoux test**. The treatment history should also record side effects of NSAIDs, DMARDs and steroids, and any serious infections on biologics.
whyNot: HLA-B27 relates to spondyloarthritis and is not a pre-biologic safety test.
Anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE and has no role in screening before a biologic.
Urate relates to gout, not biologic safety.
Schober’s test measures lumbar flexion. It is not a pre-treatment safety check.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man complains of groin pain on walking. You are screening his hips as part of a GALS examination.
questions.leadIn: Which manoeuvre most reliably shows pain and restriction early in osteoarthritis of the hip?
options: Passive internal rotation of the hip with the hip and knee flexed
Passive adduction of the straight leg
Femoral stretch test with the patient prone
Lateral compression of the anterior superior iliac spines
questions.explanation: In hip OA, **internal rotation**, abduction and extension are usually restricted. In GALS, flex the hip and knee to 90° and rotate the hip internally. **Pain and limitation appear early** in OA.
whyNot: Adduction is not among the movements typically restricted in hip OA (internal rotation, abduction, extension).
The straight leg raise tests lumbosacral nerve root irritation, not the hip joint.
The femoral stretch test detects a high lumbar disc, not hip disease.
Compressing the iliac spines stresses the sacroiliac joints.

ospe.identify: Rheumatoid hands: **ulnar deviation** at the MCPs, a **Z-shaped thumb**, **swan neck** fingers (PIP hyperextended, DIP flexed) and a **boutonnière** finger (PIP flexed, DIP hyperextended).
**Heberden’s nodes** (DIP) and **Bouchard’s nodes** (PIP): bony osteophytes of nodal osteoarthritis.
Psoriatic nail disease: **pitting**, **onycholysis**, ridging and discoloration. Look for psoriatic arthritis (DIP disease, dactylitis).
**Nail-fold infarcts** (small black-brown lesions): rheumatoid vasculitis, a sign of active disease.
Lateral cervical spine X-ray: **anterior atlanto-axial subluxation** in rheumatoid arthritis, a risk at intubation.
**Baker’s (popliteal) cyst** behind the knee. If it ruptures it mimics a DVT (crescent sign).
Joint distribution maps: **RA** symmetrical MCP/PIP/MTP; **PsA** asymmetrical PIP/DIP with entheses; **axial SpA** spine, SI and large joints; **OA** DIP, PIP, thumb base, knees and hips.

cite.figure: Clinical exam of the MSK system

ospe.identify: Spot diagnoses from inspection: **Heberden and Bouchard nodes** (OA), **RA synovitis and deformity**, **butterfly rash** (SLE), **scleritis** (RA), **acute gout**, Paget’s bowing and psoriatic nail dystrophy.
